questions.problem: What is the volume of a sphere whose diameter is $8\,\text{mm}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the volume of a sphere using the formula

$$
V=\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3},
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.

Substituting $r=\frac{8}{2}=4\,\text{mm}$ into the formula, we obtain

$$
V=\frac{4}{3}\pi \cdot {4}^{3}=\frac{256}{3}\pi \,{\text{mm}}^{3}.
$$

What is the radius of a sphere whose volume is $320\pi {\text{ cm}}^{3}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the volume of a sphere using the formula

$$
V=\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3},
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.

Substituting $V=320\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}$ into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ 320\pi  & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ 320\pi \cdot \frac{3}{4\pi } & ={r}^{3} \\ {r}^{3} & =240.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
r=\sqrt[3]{240}=2\sqrt[3]{30}\,\text{cm}.
$$

What is the radius of a sphere whose volume is $\frac{343}{6}\pi \,{\text{ft}}^{3}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the volume of a sphere using the formula

$$
V=\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3},
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.

Substituting $V=\frac{343}{6}\pi \,{\text{ft}}^{3}$ into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{343}{6}\pi  & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{343\pi \cdot 3}{6\cdot 4\pi } & ={r}^{3} \\ {r}^{3} & =\frac{343}{8} \\  & =\frac{{7}^{3}}{{2}^{3}} \\  & ={(\frac{7}{2})}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
r=\sqrt[3]{{(\frac{7}{2})}^{3}}=\frac{7}{2}\,\text{ft}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: What is the volume of a sphere whose diameter is $18 \:\textrm{cm}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can find the volume of a sphere using the formula

$$
V = \dfrac 4 3 \pi r^3 ,
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.

Substituting $r=\dfrac{18}{2}=9\:\textrm{cm}$ into the formula, we obtain

$$
V = \dfrac 4 3 \pi \left(9\right)^3 
 		= 972\pi \:\textrm{cm}^3.
$$

What is the radius of a sphere whose volume is $36\pi\:\textrm{in}^3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14234518/assets/99bb0ea67859fbd109442fcf698427ea43452087b4523b7202a760a2a8b27052.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can find the volume of a sphere using the formula

$$
V = \dfrac 4 3 \pi r^3 ,
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.

Substituting $V=36\pi\:\textrm{in}^3$ into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ 36\pi  & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ 36\pi \cdot \frac{3}{4\pi } & ={r}^{3} \\ {r}^{3} & =27.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
r = \sqrt[3]{27} = 3\:\textrm{in}.
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Given a sphere with radius $r= 3\:\textrm{cm},$ how do we calculate its volume?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14234518/assets/8df0347cb30ac58b9cbcef4b7a7e25dfd35c899b1c833cdf2e8e22bcfc51971f.png)

In general, we can find the volume of a sphere using the formula

$$
V= \dfrac 4 3 \pi r^3,
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.

Substituting $r=3\:\textrm{cm}$ into the formula, we obtain

$$
V = \dfrac 4 3 \pi \cdot (3)^3
=36 \pi \:\textrm{cm}^3.
$$

We often express the volume of a sphere as a multiple of $\pi.$ However, we can also use a calculator to get a numerical approximation. In this case, we get

$$
V \approx 113.10 \:\textrm{cm}^3
$$

rounded to two decimal places.
